newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY BANK RUN MAYBE SMEAR - OR LACK OF EXPERTISE.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY BANK RUN MAYBE SMEAR - OR LACK OF EXPERTISE.

text.p: The head of Hungary's Postabank, which lost 21 billion forints in a run by depositors, said it was the victim of a smear campaign but analysts on Monday blamed a lack of expertise among depositors.

Gabor Princz, chairman and chief executive of Hungary's second biggest bank, told Reuters in an interview that he believed the run, which began last Thursday and continued through the weekend, was the result of an organised effort.
"We are of the opinion that this was deliberately organised beforehand, the whole action, because an action like this cannot be carried out otherwise," Princz said.
"When the hysteria was going on there were some provocateurs who made announcements among the people and called up our corporate customers to make the panic stronger."

The bank called for a police investigation of the panic, which began on Thursday afternoon and soon spread to most Postabank branches throughout Budapest, prompting people to queue for hours to withdraw their money.
The bank stayed open through the weekend, during which high government officials, including National Bank of Hungary President Gyorgy Suranyi, did their best to reassure people Postabank was solvent.
On Monday the crowds were much smaller, but there were still queues at many branches.
"I'm too old to trust anything that is being said up there," said Elvira Kiss, a pensioner in her '70s, explaining why she was withdrawing her money.
Some government officials said there may have been a political motivation for the run, possibly to embarrass the Socialist government a year before elections.
During a stormy debate in Parliament, Socialist Prime Minister Gyula Horn expressed the government's confidence in Postabank, calling it a "well-functioning" institution.
But opposition Smallholders Party leader Jozsef Torgyan said the government was at fault, blaming Horn and his "dilettantism" for the bank's plight.
Financial and political analysts mostly discounted a political motivation for the panic.
"Things like (the run on Postabank) occur everywhere," said Miklos Pulai, general secretary of the Hungarian Banking Association.
"This does not show a weakness in the Hungarian banking system, but this may indicate a weakness in the whole financial culture."

Recapitalisation, technological development, the appearance of foreign banks, bank cards, ATM's and sophisticated services have raised the Hungarian banking system to among the frontrunners in central and eastern Europe.
However, the lack of public confidence in what the financial authorities say may make the management of financial crises difficult, analysts said.
"(Hungary's) financial culture is not developed enough, and hysteria can grip (banking customers)," Pulai said.
Other analysts also discounted a political motivation, saying it would have been too risky a strategy.
"I don't see how it could be politically beneficial to anyone," said political analyst Tibor Vidos. "Chaos is not something that benefits anyone."
Vidos said rumours about Postabank, which has risen dramatically on the Hungarian market since it was founded nine years ago, had circulated for some time.
"I see it as a consequence of the rumours and once they gather to a certain critical mass it explodes by itself," he said.
Bank chairman Princz said that before the run, Postabank had hoped to position itself to attract more foreign customers, but would now have to put more attention on damage control.
"Something like this never happened to us so we will have to think it over...all our international relations could be affected," he said.
